written.q: Explain why the derivative method and hill climbing are not enough for many optimisation problems, and how a population-based meta-heuristic helps.
written.a: Calculus needs f′(x) (solve f′(x*) = 0 and check the sign of f″) but for many practical problems it is intractable or cannot be computed. Hill climbing starts at one feasible solution, tries small changes and keeps the best until no lesser neighbour exists, but it is sensitive to initial conditions and can stop in a local minimum. A population-based meta-heuristic starts with many feasible solutions spread over the search space, generates new solutions in their neighbourhoods and repeats until no improvement; the best in the population at convergence is the answer, so one bad starting point does not trap the search.

written.q: Define population, chromosome, gene, allele, fitness and generation, and the three genetic operators.
written.a: Population: a group of candidate solutions; chromosome: one solution as a string; gene: one position of the string; allele: a value a gene can take (0 or 1); fitness: the objective function value (higher means better); generation: one cycle of the algorithm. Operators: selection (choose parents in proportion to fitness), crossover (swap tails of two parents at a random cut), mutation (randomly flip a gene with a very small probability).

written.q: For fitness 20, 36, 16, 84, 124, compute the roulette probabilities and explain how a computer selects a parent.
written.a: Total 280: 7.1 %, 12.9 %, 5.7 %, 30.0 %, 44.3 %. Running totals 0.071, 0.200, 0.257, 0.557, 1.000. Pick a random r in (0, 1) and choose the string whose interval contains r (r = 0.30 picks the 84; r = 0.75 picks the 124). Weak strings keep a small chance, preserving variety.

written.q: Parents 11001 and 00110 are crossed after gene 2, and then gene 4 of the first child is mutated. Show the children, the mutated child and the x values (fitness = x²).
written.a: Cut after gene 2: 11|001 and 00|110 give child 1 = 11110 (30, fitness 900) and child 2 = 00001 (1, fitness 1). Mutating gene 4 of child 1 (1 to 0) gives 11100 (28, fitness 784), slightly worse; flipping a high-value gene changes the answer a lot.

written.q: Perform one generation for Max x² with 01101, 11000, 01000, 10011 using mating pool A, B, B, D with crossovers A×B after gene 4 and B×D after gene 2 and no mutation. Compare average fitness.
written.a: Initial fitness 169, 576, 64, 361 (total 1170, average 292.5). Crossover: 01101 × 11000 after 4 gives 01100 (12) and 11001 (25); 11000 × 10011 after 2 gives 11011 (27) and 10000 (16). New fitness 144, 625, 729, 256: total 1754, average 438.5, best 729 (up from 576): the population improved.

written.q: Formulate the knapsack exercise (weights 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12 kg; values 100, 300, 200, 500, 150, 400; capacity 15 kg) as a GA: chromosome, fitness, and one iteration.
written.a: Chromosome: 6 bits (1 = pack the block). Fitness: total value if total weight ≤ 15, else 0. Example population A 110100 (900), B 010001 (700), C 001010 (350), D 100011 (22 kg, so 0). Select A and C; crossover after gene 3 gives 110010 (550) and 001100 (700); mutate gene 2 of 001100 to get 011100: blocks 3, 5, 7 kg, weight 15, value 1000, the optimum.

written.q: Why does normal crossover fail for the travelling salesman problem, and how does the random key method fix it? Decode keys 0.42, 0.06, 0.38, 0.48, 0.81.
written.a: Swapping tails of two permutations can repeat some cities and omit others (parents (1 4 3 2 5), (2 4 5 3 1) give (1 4 3 3 1)). Random keys give every city one random number in (0, 1); sort ascending to get the order, so any crossover (e.g. parameterised uniform) or mutation (immigration) on the keys always decodes to a valid route. The keys decode to the path 2 → 3 → 1 → 4 → 5.

written.q: Explain global, local and near optima and how a GA can escape a local optimum. List the termination conditions.
written.a: Global optimum: best among all solutions; local: better than neighbours but not overall; near: very close to the global optimum. A GA keeps a spread-out population, roulette selection gives weak answers a small chance, and mutation creates new gene values (e.g. flipping the first gene of 010 gives 110 = x of 6, the highest peak). Termination: a solution meets minimum criteria, fixed number of generations, budget reached, fitness plateau, manual inspection or any combination.
